company_context: Webvan was an online grocery delivery company founded in 1996 by Borders co-founder Louis Borders. It raised over $1.2 billion (including a large 1999 IPO), built automated warehouses, and expanded aggressively into multiple metro markets before filing Chapter 11 in July 2001, roughly 18 months after its IPO.
business_type: online grocery delivery startup (asset-heavy, owned fulfillment infrastructure)
evidence_summary: Webvan committed to large fixed-cost, capital-intensive automated warehouses (including a roughly $1 billion Bechtel build-out contract) and expanded to many cities before validating profitability in its first market. With an average order around $80 and a reported ~$20 loss per order, the heavy fixed-cost base and weak per-order economics combined to exhaust over $800 million and force bankruptcy.
outcome_evidence: Webvan announced shutdown and Chapter 11 filing in July 2001 (operations wound down June-July 2001), laid off about 2,000 employees, and lost more than $800 million. It is repeatedly cited as one of the largest dot-com bankruptcies.
source_limitations: The named CNN Money primary article URL returned 403 in this environment and could not be fetched directly. The figures (founding year, $1.2B raised, $800M lost, $1B Bechtel contract, $80 average order, $20 loss/order, 2,000 layoffs, July 2001 Chapter 11) were each confirmed verbatim across credible WebSearch snippets. The per-order loss is a frequently cited post-mortem estimate.
directly_stated: ~$1 billion Bechtel contract for automated fulfillment centers
inferred: Fixed-cost infrastructure scaled faster than validated demand, locking in losses
Premature multi-city expansion amplified an unproven unit economic model
why_useful_for_opsiq: Textbook strategic_capex_risk / irreversible-overexpansion case. Tests whether a system flags the danger of large, hard-to-reverse fixed-cost commitments made before unit economics are proven, and whether it recommends staged validation over blitz expansion.
